title: Why King Pekah Turned Against Judah
paragraphs: Why King Pekah Turned Against Judah
There are moments in Scripture that feel painfully modern.
Moments where political betrayal looks like family betrayal.
Moments where wounded pride becomes national destruction.
Moments where fear makes leaders forget God.
And hidden inside one of the darkest political crises in the Old Testament is a king most people barely remember.
Pekah.
A warrior king. A conspirator. A murderer. A man consumed by resistance. A ruler who turned against Judah and helped drag an entire generation toward judgment.
But if we only read his story as politics, we completely miss the warning.
Because Pekah’s rebellion was never just military.
It was spiritual.
And if we are honest… many believers are fighting the exact same war inside themselves right now.
The story unfolds during a fractured season in Israel’s history.
The united kingdom established under David and Solomon had already split in two.
The northern kingdom kept the name Israel. The southern kingdom became Judah.
Two nations. One covenant heritage. One God. But divided hearts.

The northern kingdom had descended deeper and deeper into idolatry. Its kings repeatedly abandoned the covenant of Yahweh. Altars to false gods multiplied. Political survival became more important than holiness.
And into that chaos rose Pekah.
Second Kings 15:27 says:
“In the fifty and second year of Azariah king of Judah Pekah the son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned twenty years.”
But Pekah did not inherit peace.
He seized power through assassination.
Second Kings 15:25 tells us he conspired against King Pekahiah and murdered him inside the royal palace.
This matters.
Because Scripture is showing us something deeper than politics.
Violence born from ambition rarely stays contained.
The Hebrew language quietly reveals the darkness underneath.
The word used for “conspired” is:
קָשַׁר qashar
It carries the idea of binding together secretly, treasonously, forming an unlawful alliance.
Pekah’s kingdom was built on rebellion before he ever attacked Judah.
Sin almost always spreads beyond its original target.
A compromised heart eventually becomes a compromised nation.
At first, Pekah probably looked strong. Decisive. Aggressive. Nationalistic. A defender of northern Israel.
But strength without obedience to God becomes destruction wearing armor.
The real turning point came during the reign of Ahaz king of Judah.
Ahaz was deeply compromised spiritually.
Second Kings 16 describes horrifying idolatry.
He walked “in the way of the kings of Israel.” He practiced pagan worship. He even sacrificed his own son.
Judah was spiritually weak.
And Pekah saw opportunity.
But this was bigger than opportunism.
Pekah feared Assyria.
The Assyrian Empire was becoming a terrifying superpower swallowing nations whole. Kings throughout the region were panicking.
So Pekah formed an alliance with Rezin king of Aram.
Their goal was simple: Force Judah to join their anti-Assyrian coalition.
But Ahaz refused.
And rejection ignited war.
Isaiah 7 opens with chilling tension:
“When Ahaz son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, was king of Judah, King Rezin of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel marched up to fight against Jerusalem…”
Imagine the horror.
Brother kingdoms at war. Children of Abraham attacking children of Abraham. The covenant people tearing each other apart while pagan empires watched.
The Hebrew phrase used in Isaiah 7:2 says:
וַיָּנַע לְבָבוֹ va-yaná levavo
“His heart shook.”
The text says the hearts of Ahaz and the people shook “as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.”
This is not ordinary fear.
It is terror. Political panic. Spiritual collapse. The feeling that everything is about to fall apart.
And maybe that is exactly where some people are living right now.
You smile publicly. But internally your soul is shaking.
Your marriage. Your finances. Your hidden sin. Your exhaustion. Your future. Your faith.
Everything feels unstable.
This ancient war suddenly becomes deeply personal.
Because Pekah represents something larger than himself.
He represents what happens when fear replaces trust in God.
Instead of repentance, he chose coercion. Instead of humility, he chose aggression. Instead of seeking the Lord, he trusted political force.
And humanity still does this every day.
We manipulate. We pressure. We force. We control. We panic.
Because fear convinces us God cannot be trusted with outcomes.
But then something extraordinary happens.
God sends Isaiah.
Not first to rebuke. Not first to destroy. But to invite trust.
Isaiah tells Ahaz:
“Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted…”
The Hebrew phrase:
הִשָּׁמֵר וְהַשְׁקֵט hishamer ve-hashqet
Means: “Be careful… and be still.”
That command still confronts modern believers.
Because panic has become a lifestyle.
We doom-scroll. We catastrophize. We obsess over control. We trust strategies more than surrender.
Yet God was telling Judah: You do not survive by fear. You survive by faith.
Then comes one of the most devastating prophetic lines in the entire story.
Isaiah 7:9:
“If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.”
The Hebrew uses a profound wordplay:
אִם לֹא תַאֲמִינוּ כִּי לֹא תֵאָמֵנוּ im lo ta’aminu ki lo te’amenu
“If you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all.”
The root word carries the idea of firmness, reliability, faithfulness.
Faith is not emotional denial. Faith is stability rooted in God.
And this is where Pekah ultimately failed.
He trusted alliances more than Yahweh.
He believed political unity could save him. He believed force could secure the future. He believed human power could resist judgment.
But Assyria still came.
Second Kings 15:29 records devastating loss:
“In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah… and carried them captive to Assyria.”
The empire Pekah feared became the empire that crushed him.
Fear-driven rebellion often creates the very destruction it hoped to avoid.
And eventually Pekah himself was assassinated.
The man who rose through conspiracy died through conspiracy.
Scripture is brutally honest about the cycle of sin.
Violence multiplies. Pride multiplies. Fear multiplies. Compromise multiplies.
Until entire nations collapse spiritually.
But buried inside this tragedy is something astonishing.
God still extended mercy.
Even during rebellion. Even during political corruption. Even during idolatry. Even while kingdoms trembled.
The Lord still pursued people.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because humanity has always been Pekah in some way.
We resist surrender. We grasp for control. We trust human solutions. We build alliances with sin. We fight battles without prayer.
And yet God still sends His word. Still calls us back. Still warns. Still invites repentance.
The Greek New Testament later reveals this same spiritual crisis in another form.
Romans 10:17 says:
“So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”
The Greek word for faith is:
πίστις pistis
It means trust, confidence, faithful reliance.
Not shallow positivity. Not motivational thinking.
True biblical faith is surrendering confidence into the character of God.
Pekah could not do that.
And many people today still cannot.
Some trust money more than God. Some trust politics more than God. Some trust relationships more than God. Some trust public image more than God. Some trust religious performance more than God.
But unstable foundations eventually collapse.
And maybe this article found you during your own internal civil war.
Part of you wants God. Part of you still wants control.
Part of you wants healing. Part of you still feeds hidden compromise.
Part of you wants peace. Part of you still fights battles your flesh created.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Because the tragedy of Pekah is not merely that he fought Judah.
It is that he never truly surrendered before God.
History remembers military campaigns. Heaven examines hearts.
And this is why Jesus Christ changes everything.

Where earthly kings spread fear, Christ brings peace. Where earthly rulers seize power, Christ lays His life down. Where sinful kingdoms divide, Christ reconciles. Where rebellion deserves judgment, Christ offers mercy through the cross.
The prophet Isaiah — the same prophet who confronted this crisis — would later write about the coming Messiah:
And one of His names would be:
שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם Sar-Shalom
Prince of Peace.
Not temporary political peace. Not manipulated peace. Not fear-driven peace.
True peace with God.
The kind no collapsing kingdom can destroy.
And maybe that is what your exhausted soul has actually been searching for.
Not another strategy. Not another distraction. Not another performance.
But surrender.
Jesus did not come merely to improve behavior. He came to rescue rebels.
That includes fearful people. Proud people. Religious people. Broken people. Compromised people.
People like Pekah. People like Ahaz. People like us.
Some people are losing wars internally while pretending everything is fine publicly.
One day every kingdom built on fear will fall… but every soul anchored in Christ will still stand.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Tinalikuran ni Haring Pekah ang Juda
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na parang balita ngayon.
Mga panahong ang pagkakanulo sa politika ay parang pagkakanulo ng sariling pamilya.
Mga panahong ang takot ay mas malakas kaysa pananampalataya.
Mga panahong ang mga tao ng Diyos mismo ang naglalaban-laban.
At nakatago sa isa sa pinakamadilim na krisis ng Lumang Tipan ang isang haring halos hindi naaalala ng marami.
Si Pekah.
Isang mandirigma. Isang traydor. Isang mamamatay-tao. Isang haring nalunod sa paghihimagsik.
Ngunit kung politika lang ang makikita natin sa kanyang kwento… mamimiss natin ang tunay na babala.
Dahil ang laban ni Pekah laban sa Juda ay hindi lang militar.
Espirituwal ito.
At kung magiging totoo tayo… maraming tao ngayon ang may parehong digmaan sa loob ng puso nila.
Nagsimula ang lahat matapos mabiyak ang kaharian ni Solomon.
Ang hilagang kaharian ay tinawag na Israel. Ang timog naman ay Juda.
Iisang kasaysayan. Iisang Diyos. Ngunit hati ang puso.
Habang lumilipas ang panahon, mas lumalalim ang hilagang Israel sa idolatriya.
Ang mga hari nito ay paulit-ulit na tumalikod kay Yahweh. Mas naging mahalaga ang kapangyarihan kaysa kabanalan. Mas naging mahalaga ang kaligtasan ng kaharian kaysa pagsunod sa Diyos.
At sa gitna ng kaguluhang iyon, umangat si Pekah.
Ngunit hindi siya naging hari sa mapayapang paraan.
Sa 2 Hari 15:25, makikita natin na nakipagsabwatan siya laban kay Haring Pekahias at pinatay niya ito sa loob mismo ng palasyo.
Mahalagang detalye iyon.
Dahil ipinapakita ng Kasulatan na ang kahariang itinayo sa paghihimagsik ay bihirang magtapos sa kapayapaan.
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “nakipagsabwatan” ay:
קָשַׁר qashar
Ibig sabihin nito ay lihim na pagbuo ng pagtataksil. Pagkakaisa para sa rebelyon.
Bago pa lusubin ni Pekah ang Juda… may digmaan na sa loob ng kanyang puso.
At ganiyan din minsan ang tao.
Ang kasalanang kinukubli ay hindi nananatiling maliit.
Unti-unti nitong winawasak ang isip. Ang relasyon. Ang tahanan. Ang pananampalataya.
Noong una, maaaring mukhang malakas si Pekah. Matapang. Makabayan. Isang lider na handang lumaban.
Pero ang lakas na walang pagsunod sa Diyos ay nagiging pagkawasak na may suot na baluti.
Dumating ang pinakamahalagang bahagi ng kwento noong panahon ni Ahaz, hari ng Juda.
Si Ahaz ay espirituwal na mahina.
Ayon sa 2 Hari 16, lumakad siya sa kasalanan ng mga hari ng Israel. Sumamba siya sa mga diyus-diyosan. At mas masakit… inihandog pa niya ang sarili niyang anak.
Mahina ang Juda. At nakita iyon ni Pekah.
Pero may mas malalim pang dahilan.
Takot si Pekah.
Takot siya sa lumalakas na imperyo ng Asiria.
Sinakop ng Asiria ang mga bansa isa-isa. Lahat ng hari noon ay nangangamba.
Kaya nakipag-alyansa si Pekah kay Haring Rezin ng Aram.
Ang plano nila? Piliting sumama ang Juda sa kanilang laban kontra Asiria.
Pero tumanggi si Ahaz.
At doon nagsimula ang digmaan.
Sa Isaias 7, sinabi:
“Si Rezin na hari ng Siria at si Pekah na anak ni Remalias ay umahon laban sa Jerusalem upang salakayin iyon…”
Isipin mo iyon.
Magkapatid na kaharian. Mga anak ni Abraham. Ngunit nagpapatayan.
Habang pinapanood sila ng mga paganong imperyo.
Sinasabi ng Isaias 7:2:
וַיָּנַע לְבָבוֹ va-yaná levavo
“Nanginig ang kanyang puso.”
Hindi ito ordinaryong takot.
Ito iyong klase ng takot na parang mawawasak na ang lahat.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na ganiyan ang nararamdaman.
Ngumingiti ka sa harap ng iba. Pero sa loob… pagod na pagod ka na.
Takot ka sa mangyayari sa pamilya mo. Takot ka sa kinabukasan. Takot ka sa kasalanang hindi mo mabitawan. Takot ka na baka lumalayo ka na sa Diyos.
At biglang nagiging personal ang kwento ni Pekah.
Dahil si Pekah ay larawan ng taong pinamumunuan ng takot kaysa pagtitiwala sa Diyos.
Sa halip na magsisi… nanakot siya. Sa halip na magpakumbaba… lumaban siya. Sa halip na hanapin si Yahweh… umasa siya sa politika at kapangyarihan.
At hanggang ngayon, ginagawa pa rin iyon ng tao.
Kinokontrol natin ang lahat. Pinipilit natin ang gusto natin. Nagpapanic tayo. Nag-ooverthink tayo.
Dahil minsan… hindi talaga tayo nagtitiwala na kayang hawakan ng Diyos ang buhay natin.
Pero dito naging makapangyarihan ang kwento.
Nagpadala ang Diyos ng propeta.
Hindi agad para manira. Hindi agad para humatol.
Kundi para tawagin silang magtiwala.
Sinabi ni Isaias kay Ahaz:
“Mag-ingat ka at manahimik ka; huwag kang matakot…”
Sa Hebreo:
הִשָּׁמֵר וְהַשְׁקֵט hishamer ve-hashqet
“Mag-ingat… at maging payapa.”
Napakalalim ng utos na iyon.
Dahil maraming Kristiyano ngayon ang nabubuhay sa panic.
Laging balisa. Laging natatakot. Laging may iniisip.
Pero sinasabi pa rin ng Diyos: Hindi ka mabubuhay sa takot. Mabubuhay ka sa pananampalataya.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang isa sa pinakamabibigat na talata sa kwento.
Isaias 7:9:
“Kung hindi kayo mananampalataya, tiyak na hindi kayo matatatag.”
Sa Hebreo:
אִם לֹא תַאֲמִינוּ כִּי לֹא תֵאָמֵנוּ im lo ta’aminu ki lo te’amenu
Kung wala kang pananampalataya… wala kang matatag na pundasyon.
At dito tuluyang nabigo si Pekah.
Mas nagtiwala siya sa alyansa kaysa kay Yahweh. Mas naniwala siya sa lakas ng tao kaysa sa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Pero dumating pa rin ang Asiria.
Sa 2 Hari 15:29, sinakop nila ang mga lungsod ng Israel at dinala ang mga tao bilang bihag.
Ang kinatatakutan ni Pekah… iyon mismo ang sumira sa kanya.
Ganiyan minsan ang buhay.
Kapag takot ang nagpapatakbo sa atin, madalas tayo mismo ang gumagawa ng pagkawasak na gusto nating iwasan.
At kalaunan… pinaslang din si Pekah.
Ang taong umangat sa pamamagitan ng pagtataksil ay bumagsak din sa parehong paraan.
Napakatapat ng Biblia.
Ang kasalanan ay lumalaki. Ang pride ay lumalaki. Ang takot ay lumalaki.
Hanggang sa bumagsak ang buong tao.
Pero kahit sa gitna ng kaguluhan… may awa pa rin ang Diyos.
Iyon ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo.
Dahil kahit paulit-ulit tayong pumapalya… patuloy pa rin Siyang tumatawag.
Patuloy Siyang nagbababala. Patuloy Siyang naghihintay. Patuloy Siyang nag-aalok ng kapatawaran.
At dito pumapasok si Jesucristo.
Dahil ang problema ng tao ay hindi lang politika. Hindi lang emosyon. Hindi lang trauma.
Kasalanan.
At si Jesus ang dumating para iligtas ang mga rebelde.
Mga takot. Mga pagod. Mga nagtatago. Mga wasak. Mga taong pilit kinokontrol ang lahat.
Mga taong katulad natin.
Sinasabi sa Roma 10:17:
“Ang pananampalataya ay nanggagaling sa pakikinig, at ang pakikinig ay sa pamamagitan ng salita ng Diyos.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “pananampalataya” ay:
πίστις pistis
Ibig sabihin: Buong pagtitiwala. Buong pag-asa. Buong pagsandal.
Hindi fake positivity. Hindi pagpapanggap na okay ka.
Kundi tunay na pagsuko sa Diyos.
At baka iyon talaga ang kailangan mo ngayon.
Hindi panibagong distraction. Hindi panibagong kontrol. Hindi panibagong pagtatago.
Kundi pagsuko.
Dahil habang ang mga hari sa lupa ay nagdadala ng takot… si Cristo ay nagdadala ng kapayapaan.
Habang ang mundo ay naghahati-hati… si Jesus ay nagkakasundo.
Habang ang kasalanan ay sumisira… si Cristo ay nagliligtas.
At ang parehong propetang si Isaias na nakakita ng kaguluhan ni Pekah ay nagsulat din tungkol sa darating na Mesiyas.
Tinawag niya Siyang:
שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם Sar-Shalom
Prinsipe ng Kapayapaan.
Hindi pansamantalang kapayapaan. Hindi kapayapaang gawa ng politika.
Kundi tunay na kapayapaan sa Diyos.
At kapag si Cristo ang pundasyon mo… kahit gaano kalakas ang bagyo, mananatili kang nakatayo.
May mga taong mukhang okay sa labas pero wasak na pala sa loob.
Darating ang araw na lahat ng kahariang itinayo sa takot ay babagsak… pero ang pusong nakatanim kay Cristo ay mananatiling nakatayo.
